title: Multiple Integration
body:
Integrating over a region of space rather than an interval, done by iterating one-variable
integrals: hold everything else fixed, integrate the innermost variable, work outward. The exact
inverse of taking a [[Partial Derivative]], one variable at a time.

> **Split with [[CALCULUS 2]]**: MRU teaches **double** integrals in Calculus 2 and **triple**
> integrals here, so [[Double Integral]] owns the plane case and this note owns
> $\iiint_E f\,dV$ and the general machinery. That is an unusual boundary and worth remembering
> when looking for a formula.

## Triple integrals

$$
\iiint_E f(x,y,z)\,dV = \int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} \int_{h_1(x,y)}^{h_2(x,y)} f\,dz\,dy\,dx
$$

The limits are read **inside out**: the innermost may depend on both outer variables, the middle on
the outermost only, and the outermost must be constants. If an outer limit still contains a
variable, the setup is wrong. Getting the limits right is the whole problem; the integration itself
is [[Integration Techniques]] from Calc 2.

With $f = 1$ it gives volume, the same way a double integral with $f=1$ gives area. With $f = \rho$
a density it gives mass, and moments over mass give the centre of mass, which is
[[Applications of Integration]] with the slicing done properly.

## Fubini's theorem

For a continuous integrand on a reasonable region, **the order of integration does not change the
answer**. That is permission to reorder, and reordering is the main technique: a triple integral
has six possible orders and it is common for one to be elementary and the other five to be
unpleasant. Sketching the region is what tells you which.

## Change of variables

$$
\iiint_E f\,dV = \iiint_{E'} f(\mathbf{x}(u,v,w)) \left| \frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)} \right| du\,dv\,dw
$$

The **Jacobian** is the [[Determinant]] of the matrix of partials, and it is there because a change
of coordinates stretches volume locally by exactly that factor. This is the same statement
[[Determinant]] makes in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (a determinant is a volume scaling), applied
point by point rather than once, so the two courses are describing one fact.

| Coordinates | Volume element | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| Cartesian | $dx\,dy\,dz$ | boxes |
| Cylindrical | $r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz$ | circular symmetry about an axis |
| Spherical | $\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$ | spherical symmetry |

The $r$ in cylindrical is the same $r$ that makes [[Polar Coordinates|polar]] area
$\int\int r\,dr\,d\theta$, and the $\rho^2\sin\phi$ is its three-dimensional counterpart. **The
extra factor is not a convention to memorise, it is the Jacobian**, and forgetting it is the
standard error.
